items.author: Jonathan Kemper
items.article_content:
Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.

### Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.

### Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion, which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like Computer and its always-on Teammates, along with developer tools like Search as Code.

items.article_content_en:
Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.

### Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.

### Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

items.title_zh: Perplexity推出Monitor API支持自动化实时监控
items.summary_zh: Perplexity发布Monitor API，通过自定义自然语言目标实现对全网及特定页面的自动化监控与智能筛选更新
items.article_content_zh:
Perplexity 正在通过新的 API 扩展其开发人员业务，该 API 仅在发生相关变化时才唤醒代理。

Perplexity 的新 Monitor API 按计划监视网络，并通过 webhook 向应用程序和代理发送更新。到目前为止，工程团队必须自己触发重复搜索并维护自定义代码以删除重复项并检测更改。 Perplexity 表示，这种方法几乎不可能在数百个主题和页面上维护。

API 有两种模式。网络监视器定期通过 Perplexity 的网络和新闻搜索运行搜索查询，以捕捉人工智能基础设施公司新一轮融资等动态。页面监视器最多跟踪 10 个页面，例如定价页面、变更日志或策略。在第一次运行时，它们存储基线版本并返回此后任何更改的文本差异。

### 决策模型过滤掉不重要的结果

Perplexity 根据开发人员用自然语言定义的目标，使用自己的决策模型来评估结果。网络搜索结果必须明确检查相关性、来源可信度、新颖性和及时性，而页面更改则根据其是否对目标重要来判断。仅当满足每个阈值时，服务才会发送带有置信度分数的更新。开发人员可以单独调整每个检查的阈值并更改目标，而无需重新创建监视器。

监视器按照每 15 分钟一次到每周一次的计划运行，或者按照自定义的 cron 计划运行。每次运行都会从上一次停止的地方继续，并且服务会过滤掉重复的结果。 Webhooks 已签名，并且 Perplexity 在出现临时错误后会自动重试传递。开发人员可以通过 API 或 API 控制台暂停、恢复或手动触发监视器。

### Perplexity 声称在内部测试中处于领先地位

Perplexity 针对 Firecrawl、Exa 和 Parallel 的监控服务测试了其 API，涵盖了来自真实搜索 API 查询的 60 个主题，包括公司新闻、技术发布和监管。每个提供商都有自己的时间表和设置，并且有一个单独的模型根据相关性和新近度对每个结果进行评分。

Perplexity 表示，在前 8 个小时内，它交付了 63 个新鲜的相关页面，而 Firecrawl 为 20 个，Exa 为 15 个，Parallel Core 和 Lite 各为 10 个。困惑将这些数字描述为早期的内部结果。这三个竞争对手在 8 月份的人工智能代理传统搜索 API 人工分析基准测试中处于领先地位，尽管 Perplexity 并未包含在该测试中。

困惑指向使用案例，例如销售团队跟踪目标客户的融资轮次和人员变动，以及分析师关注季度收益和收购。其他代理旨在标记竞争对手的价格变化或为合规团队总结新的监管规则。

Web 监视器每 1,000 次成功运行的成本为 1 美元，页面监视器每 1,000 个获取的 URL 的成本为 1 美元。 Monitor API 现在可通过 API 和 API 控制台使用，并使用与搜索、上下文和代理 API 相同的密钥。

Perplexity 是最早的人工智能搜索引擎之一，但网络搜索从此成为 ChatGPT、Claude 和 Gemini 等聊天机器人的标准功能。 8 月份，The Information 报道称，英伟达正在洽谈估值超过 300 亿美元的投资，这意味着 Perplexity 需要找到有利可图的商业模式。该公司正在押注于像 Computer 及其永远在线的 Teammates 这样的代理，以及像 Search as Code 这样的开发工具。

items.title: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
items.title_en: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns

inline_images.caption: METR's analysis shows the steady rise in capabilities of leading AI models up through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. | Image: METR
inline_images.caption_en: METR's analysis shows the steady rise in capabilities of leading AI models up through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. | Image: METR

items.author: Matthias Bastian
items.article_content:
AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

人工智能模型在人工智能研究任务中正在迅速改进，而且它们变得越来越难以衡量。人工智能研究组织 METR 表示，当前的公开数据不足以排除未来几年人工智能研究急剧加速的可能性。该组织警告说，这可能会让人类无法“有意义地理解、评估和应对新人工智能系统带来的灾难性风险”。

METR 发现，在具有直接反馈的明确定义的编码和计算任务上，这些模型在大多数情况下已经击败了经验丰富的人类专业人士，尽管它们还没有超过大批顶级专家。对于人类需要更长时间的任务，模型可以处理的任务长度每 3.6 个月就会增加一倍。根据 METR 数据的简单推断，到 2027 年 7 月，他们完成最长 200 小时任务的成功率为 50%。

items.title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
items.title_en: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
items.author: David Pierce
items.article_content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.

Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.

The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.

Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.

In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotakuthat the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.

All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”

The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want?

ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solidon the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list.

The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.

Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.

At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.

But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which lots of people are doing) or your computer (which lots of people are also doing), do it carefully. And make lots of backups.

If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund.

You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on Waveshare, which has a big selection and pretty good prices.

Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called ESP-Claw. It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler.

Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi… to hack a Raspberry Pi.

Check out Terrence O’Brien’s deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear.

Elektor has a good piece about the history and technical details of ESP32, which goes back more than a decade.

Richie at Fuji X Weekly posted a follow-up to that original blog about vibe-coded firmware, diving into both the debate about AI in general and about what it even means to use a particular camera. “If that camera can be hacked with AI vibe coded 3rd party firmware to change its functions and features, is it still the same camera?”

Just as AI is being used to revive and improve old gadgets, The Verge’s Andrew Webster found that so too are old games being reimagined with AI. For better and for worse.

I wrote a while back about the personal software revolution and how vibe coding meant everyone could build the exact software they want. The same thing is coming fast to hardware everywhere.

Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.

Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the Muse Gadgets program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.

At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.

But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which lots of people are doing) or your computer (which lots of people are also doing), do it carefully. And make lots of backups.

If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund.

You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on Waveshare, which has a big selection and pretty good prices.

Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called ESP-Claw. It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler.

Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi… to hack a Raspberry Pi.

Check out Terrence O’Brien’s deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear.

Elektor has a good piece about the history and technical details of ESP32, which goes back more than a decade.

Richie at Fuji X Weekly posted a follow-up to that original blog about vibe-coded firmware, diving into both the debate about AI in general and about what it even means to use a particular camera. “If that camera can be hacked with AI vibe coded 3rd party firmware to change its functions and features, is it still the same camera?”

Just as AI is being used to revive and improve old gadgets, The Verge’s Andrew Webster found that so too are old games being reimagined with AI. For better and for worse.

I wrote a while back about the personal software revolution and how vibe coding meant everyone could build the exact software they want. The same thing is coming fast to hardware everywhere.
paragraphs: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.

Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.

The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.

Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.

In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotakuthat the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.

All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”

(Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want?

ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see real-time sea conditions, rig up a monitor for your whole DJ system, or just play Metal Gear Solidon the go. You can even have a dedicated device for your family’s shopping list.

items.title_zh: 大模型“意念编程”开启消费电子硬件破解潮
items.summary_zh: 开发者利用Claude Code等AI工具简化硬件底层代码交互，Android设备的非官方界面定制与功能解锁正加速普及

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 基于大型语言模型（LLM）的新型硬件定制方式正在兴起，开发者通过调用Claude Code或Codex等工具，降低了对各类消费级硬件进行底层配置与界面改造的门槛。以Android TV设备为例，通过自动化的USB调试权限管理与代码修改，用户可轻松去除系统广告并重构用户界面，此类名为“意念编程（vibe-coding）”的实践已引发开源社区对设备掌控权的市场性反思与功能解锁风潮。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: A new wave of hardware customization, termed 'vibe-coding,' is emerging as developers utilize large language models like Claude Code and Codex to simplify low-level hardware configuration. By automating interactions such as modifying Android TV interfaces and bypassing bloatware via USB debugging, this trend is significantly lowering the barrier for end-user control over proprietary hardware, fueling a grassroots movement for open-device ecosystems.

elements_zh.who: 软件开发者（以Gathin T为代表）及Claude Code用户
elements_zh.where: 消费电子设备（以Android TV为代表）的个性化与改装领域
elements_zh.what: 利用AI模型简化底层代码交互，实现系统广告屏蔽与界面定制化重构
elements_zh.why: AI极大地降低了硬件逆向工程与系统调整的技术门槛，增强了消费者对设备的实际掌控权

elements_en.who: Software developers (e.g., Gathin T) and Claude Code users
elements_en.where: Customization and modification of consumer electronics (Android TV platforms)
elements_en.what: Using AI models to simplify low-level coding interactions for ad-blocking and UI restructuring
elements_en.why: AI lowers the barrier for hardware reverse engineering and customization, empowering consumer device autonomy

ai_analysis.insight_zh: AI赋能的底层代码交互实际上是对消费电子“黑盒化”商业模式的降维打击。当LLM使得逆向工程和固件修补不再依赖专业知识时，厂商通过封锁系统API维护护城河的策略将失效，迫使硬件生态必须转向更开放的软件服务竞争，否则将面临大规模的用户端“去中心化”改造挑战。
ai_analysis.insight_en: AI-empowered low-level coding effectively disrupts the 'black box' business model of consumer electronics. As LLMs lower the barriers to reverse engineering, vendor strategies that lock system APIs to maintain moats will become obsolete, forcing a shift towards open ecosystem competition to prevent widespread user-led decentralization of proprietary systems.

items.article_content_zh:
这是《The Stepback》，一份每周简讯，详细介绍了科技界的一个重要故事。有关一切事物的振动黑客的更多信息，请关注大卫·皮尔斯。 《Stepback》将于美国东部时间周日上午 8 点到达我们订阅者的收件箱。在此处选择加入“后退”。

就像人工智能的许多事情一样，大型语言模型并不是开辟了某种全新的功能。自从小工具出现以来，一些用户就一直在对它们进行黑客攻击、改装、越狱，并根据自己的喜好进行调整。新鲜的是现在很容易了。世界各地的人们发现，他们只需提示 Claude Code 或 Codex 即可使用大型语言模型来破解他们的硬件。它导致了开发人员友好型小工具的繁荣，并为您能想到的几乎所有设备上的更好软件创造了市场。

对于一位名叫 Gathin T 的印度开发商来说，整个事情的开始几乎是一时兴起。 “有一天下午，我正在摆弄电视，它真的很糟糕，”他告诉我。他的电视机是小米制作的，运行Android TV，广告太多，界面混乱，甚至很难更改输入。他开始思考：如果你可以在你的 Android 手机上安装另一个启动器，也许你也可以在你的电视上做同样的事情。 “我想到的第一件事就是从电视上删除过时的软件，”他说。 “然后我想，为什么不让它看起来更好呢？”

Gathin 提示 Claude Code 并发现，通过一些权限调整和 USB 调试模式切换，他的聊天机器人可以控制他的电视，只要它们位于同一个 Wi-Fi 网络上。一个半小时后，加辛按照自己的喜好重新设计了电视——屏幕上不再有广告，界面更简单，通过其他输入更容易访问他的 PlayStation。他在 X 上发布了自己的所作所为，并迅速走红。因此，Gathin 整理了他的工作，购买了一个域名，并推出了 CleanYourTV 作为帮助其他人解决自己的电视界面问题的工具。它成为 GitHub 上最受欢迎的存储库之一，收到了数以千计的拉取请求和功能创意，并激发了无数人将自己的聊天机器人指向他们的大屏幕。

Gathin 小心翼翼地指出，唯一能如此轻松运行的电视是基于 Android 的电视。 （他通过其他操作系统进行了 Claude Code 破解，但这些涉及更明确的越狱和 root，因此他更不愿意如此广泛地分享该过程。）但对于世界各地的氛围黑客来说，好消息是 Android 可以运行一切。从洗碗机到数码相框再到豪华汽车，即使是看起来不像 Android 的小工具也通常运行 Android。即使他们不这样做，也很可能有另一种方法。如果有隐藏的 API，您的法学硕士可以找到它。如果固件文件位于某个网站上，您的法学硕士可以将其解压、探索并根据您的喜好重新打包。

同样，这里的技术功能很少是新的，有进取心的开发人员多年来一直在从事此类工作。有些人甚至已经使用人工智能好几年了，以使工作变得更轻松。但当 Claude Code 在 2025 年底首次出现“天哪，它有用”的时刻时，开发人员开始更加依赖这些工具，非开发人员开始发现他们现在也可以构建软件。 2026 年，越来越多的人开始将这种功能指向他们的硬件。

现在看来，所有硬件都是黑客硬件。相机爱好者和任何人一样快地接受了氛围黑客的可能性，利用法学硕士以各种方式重新打包他们的相机软件。像 Magic Lantern 这样的固件黑客是相机社区的主要内容，但突然之间，似乎每个人都在使用人工智能来添加新的录制功能，支持更高分辨率，甚至为他们的照片添加新的外观和颜色配置文件。许多人正在使用这些工具来赋予他们的旧装备新的生命；其他更有进取心的氛围编码员正在将他们的机器人指向他们的全新硬件。

音乐世界也同样被颠覆。崭露头角的音乐家正在将廉价的合成器转变为强大的新型装备，而一种名为 M-Vave FM-1 的廉价小工具已成为定制固件和新功能的热门目标。 M-Vave 甚至发布了一个开源固件，拥抱黑客，而其他公司则试图将他们拒之门外。 FM-1 价格便宜，很容易被破解，这引发了人们对高端制造商如何才能参与竞争的疑问。

游戏玩家还使用人工智能来反编译和修改他们喜欢的游戏，他们正在使用法学硕士为他们的游戏机添加新功能。一位 vivi 编码员找到了一种在 PlayStation 5 上播放 PlayStation 2 光盘的方法；许多游戏玩家构建了脚本，允许他们在其他设备上使用自己喜欢的控制器。

特别是在游戏领域，这引起了业界的反击。游戏制作者正在寻找方法来保护他们的作品不被反编译并在其他平台上免费提供。长期担任游戏高管、最近担任 Take-Two 人工智能主管的卢克·迪肯 (Luke Dicken) 最近向 Kotaku 预测，该行业将开始采用“更具侵入性的 DRM、平台级解决方案，并且可能会更多地推动流媒体解决方案，因为没有人可以反编译他们无法获得的东西。”硬件制造商将更加努力地锁定他们的系统；所有公司都将采取法律行动来保护其知识产权。

所有这些硬件访问也给用户带来了新的风险。当您安装相机固件的 vivi 编码版本时，您现在就远远超出了相机制造商可以帮助您解决的范围。您可能会被要求克劳德解决克劳德造成的问题所困扰。正如 Ritchie Roesch 最近在《Fuji X Weekly》上所写的那样，“重要的不是某人的相机是否会成为永久的镇纸，而是何时、有多少，以及是否属于你的问题。”

对于有进取心的氛围黑客来说，更安全（且更少诉讼）的途径在于一种全新的硬件。 ESP32 模块将网络芯片、麦克风、扬声器等封装到一个简单且对黑客友好的包中，突然在硬件社区中无处不在。 （想想 Raspberry Pi，但更便宜、更通用。）当然，您可以使用 Claude Code 对 Kindle 进行越狱和去亚马逊化，但当您可以购买像 M5Stack PaperMono 这样的设备时，为什么还要这么做呢？ M5Stack PaperMono 是一种基于 ESP32 的电子纸设备，您可以将其制作成任何您想要的东西呢？

ESP32 模块非常适合帮助您构建 Apple 或三星永远不会考虑的超特定设备。只需几美元和一些提示，您就可以构建一种查看实时海况的方法，为您的整个 DJ 系统安装一个监视器，或者只是随时随地播放 Metal Gear Solidon。您甚至可以为家人的购物清单配备专用设备。

设备制造商和振动黑客之间的军备竞赛只会继续下去。随着人工智能模型变得越来越强大，工具和用户都变得越来越复杂，任何人都将越来越容易地将他们的机器人指向他们的电视、汽车或洗衣机，看看会发生什么。一些制造商会尽力将黑客拒之门外；其他人会寻找安全拥抱它们的方法。一些用户会发现他们的技术令人难以置信的新功能；其他人会发现他们创造了非常大且昂贵的镇纸。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】软件开发者（以Gathin T为代表）及Claude Code用户：利用AI模型简化底层代码交互，实现系统广告屏蔽与界面定制化重构
【起因与机理】AI极大地降低了硬件逆向工程与系统调整的技术门槛，增强了消费者对设备的实际掌控权
【关键技术规格】AI模型大幅降低了硬件底层配置与修改的技术门槛。
【各方立场与态度】消费电子市场将面临从单一控制权向用户自定义权力的生态演变。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Software developers (e.g., Gathin T) and Claude Code users: Using AI models to simplify low-level coding interactions for ad-blocking and UI restructuring
[Root Cause & Mechanism] AI lowers the barrier for hardware reverse engineering and customization, empowering consumer device autonomy
[Key Technical Spec] AI models significantly reduce technical barriers for low-level hardware configuration and modification.
[Key Position & Outlook] Consumer electronics markets face a shift from proprietary control to user-driven customization.

One last round, chads.

The 4th and final epoch of @termix_ai has officially started.

It's been a pretty interesting journey so far.

From exploring AACP and minting my own onchain agent identity to diving into agent reputation, verification mechanisms and autonomous trading strategies.

I started this campaign out of curiosity and ended up finishing #3 in Epoch 1 and #1 in Epoch 2.

But we're not done yet.

For the final epoch, I'll keep exploring the technical side of TermiX, sharing my own takes and breaking down what an actual autonomous agent economy could look like.

There's still a lot to unpack beyond the usual AI agent hype.

Let's make this last epoch count.

One final push. No slowing down now.

See you on the leaderboard, anons.

items.quote_en:
One last round, chads.

The 4th and final epoch of @termix_ai has officially started.

It's been a pretty interesting journey so far.

From exploring AACP and minting my own onchain agent identity to diving into agent reputation, verification mechanisms and autonomous trading strategies.

I started this campaign out of curiosity and ended up finishing #3 in Epoch 1 and #1 in Epoch 2.

But we're not done yet.

For the final epoch, I'll keep exploring the technical side of TermiX, sharing my own takes and breaking down what an actual autonomous agent economy could look like.

There's still a lot to unpack beyond the usual AI agent hype.

Let's make this last epoch count.

One final push. No slowing down now.

See you on the leaderboard, anons.

items.title_en:
Demon Slayer, Street Fighter and Shield Hero Voice Actor, Stephen Fu Celebrates 41! 🎙️🔥🎮

Stephen Fu has quickly become a familiar voice across modern anime and gaming, bringing a striking range of heroes, villains, and fan favorites to life. His chilling performance as Douma in Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba stands alongside major game roles like Iron Fist / Lin Lie in Marvel Rivals, Jamie in Street Fighter 6, and Hwei in League of Legends.

Anime fans also know him as Naofumi Iwatani in The Rising of the Shield Hero, Weather Report in JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Stone Ocean, Sakuta Azusagawa in Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai, and Lance Crown in Mashle: Magic and Muscles. Newer roles such as Anaxa in Honkai: Star Rail, Natsuki Seba in Sakamoto Days, and Naito Mudano in Tougen Anki continue to expand an already impressive résumé.

Some of his most notable voice roles include:
• Douma — Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
• Iron Fist / Lin Lie — Marvel Rivals
• Jamie — Street Fighter 6
• Cho Sang-woo — Squid Game
• Naofumi Iwatani — The Rising of the Shield Hero
• Hwei — League of Legends
• Wise — Zenless Zone Zero
• Weather Report — JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Stone Ocean
• Sakuta Azusagawa — Rascal Does Not Dream of Bunny Girl Senpai
• Anaxa — Honkai: Star Rail
• Lance Crown — Mashle: Magic and Muscles
• Henry Legolant — Black Clover
• Seiji Shishikura — My Hero Academia
• Ryo Saeba — City Hunter
• Noé Archiviste — The Case Study of Vanitas
• Shinpei Ajiro — Summer Time Rendering
• Akito Yamada — My Love Story with Yamada-kun at Lv999
• Natsuki Seba — Sakamoto Days
• Naito Mudano — Tougen Anki
• Khrome Ryugu — Beyblade X

With roles spanning intense villains, laid-back leads, fighters, and emotionally complex heroes, Fu continues to make his mark across some of anime and gaming’s biggest worlds.

Happy 41st Birthday, Stephen Fu! 🎂✨

鬼灭之刃、街头霸王、盾牌英雄配音演员傅士芬庆祝 41 岁生日！ 🎙️🔥🎮

史蒂芬·傅 (Stephen Fu) 迅速成为现代动漫和游戏领域的知名人物，将一系列引人注目的英雄、反派和粉丝最爱的角色带入生活。他在《鬼灭之刃》中饰演 Douma 的令人毛骨悚然的表演，与《漫威对手》中的铁拳 / 林烈、《街头霸王 6》中的 Jamie 以及《英雄联盟》中的 Hwei 等主要游戏角色齐名。

动漫迷们还知道他在《盾之勇者成名录》中扮演岩谷尚文、在《JoJo的奇妙冒险：石之海》中扮演天气预报、在《青春猪头少年不会梦到兔女郎学姐》中的梓川咲太以及在《魔法与肌肉》中扮演兰斯·克朗。新角色，如《崩坏：星轨》中的阿那克萨、《坂本时代》中的濑叶夏希以及《桃源 Anki》中的内藤·穆达诺，继续扩大本已令人印象深刻的履历。

他的一些最著名的配音角色包括：
• Douma — 鬼灭之刃：Kimetsu no Yaiba
• 铁拳 / 林烈 — Marvel Rivals
• 杰米 — 街头霸王 6
• Cho Sang-woo — 鱿鱼游戏
• 岩谷尚文 — 《盾之勇者成名录》
• Hwei — 英雄联盟
• Wise — Zenless 零区
• 天气预报 — JoJo的奇妙冒险：石之海
• 梓川咲太 — 青春猪头少年不会梦到兔女郎学姐
• Anaxa — 崩坏：星轨
• Lance Crown — Mashle：魔法与肌肉
• 亨利·莱戈兰特——《黑色四叶草》
• 狮子仓精二 — 我的英雄学院
• Ryo Saeba — 城市猎人
• Noé Archiviste — Vanitas 案例研究
• Shinpei Ajiro — 夏季渲染
• Akito Yamada — 我与山田君的爱情故事 Lv999
• 濑场夏希 — 坂本时代
• 内藤·穆达诺 — Tougen Anki
• Khrome Ryugu — Beyblade X

傅的角色涵盖激烈的反派、悠闲的主角、战士和情感复杂的英雄，他继续在动漫和游戏的一些最大的世界中留下自己的印记。

傅士芬 41 岁生日快乐！ 🎂✨

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 百度官方宣布文心大模型ERNIE 5.5 Flash预览版现已通过vLLM-ERNIE插件获得vLLM框架的即时（Day-0）支持。该模型采用280B总参数量与14B激活参数的混合专家（MoE）架构，具备推理与工具调用能力，并支持高达100万token的长文本上下文处理。

elements_zh.what: 发布vLLM-ERNIE插件支持ERNIE 5.5 Flash模型，支持1M token长窗口

elements_en.what: Launched vLLM-ERNIE plugin for ERNIE 5.5 Flash, enabling 1M token context
elements_en.why: To improve deployment performance and ecosystem compatibility via open-source inference standards

ai_analysis.insight_zh: ERNIE系列通过接入vLLM插件，实质上是百度在开源推理基础设施层面的生态卡位，旨在降低开发者在其MoE模型上的落地门槛。此举不仅是对抗同类长上下文模型竞争的差异化策略，更是通过与主流推理框架的深度绑定，加速其模型在私有化部署市场的份额渗透。
ai_analysis.insight_en: By integrating with the vLLM plugin, Baidu is strategically securing its position within the open-source inference ecosystem to lower barriers for MoE model deployment. This move serves as a competitive play against other long-context models, aiming to accelerate market penetration in private deployment by aligning with standardized inference infrastructures.

items.title_en:
He's right.  We are experiencing the death of thought.

Just now, I had to read a hefty AI-generated 900-word post about a guy who printed a contract and used a mechanical pencil.

Rather than skim it for 12 seconds, whisper “good for him,” and move on with my evening, I did something radical.

I didn’t print your post on a Wi-Fi laser printer like some kind of Silicon Valley soft-hands.

I transcribed every single one of your 902 words by hand onto unbleached calfskin vellum using a goose quill I cured in my own garage, sharpened it with a dull pocketknife until my thumb bled, and spent four and a half hours marking up the margins in homemade iron-gall ink.

I finished writing down my thoughts in the margins, set down my quill, stared silently at a brass lamp, and reflected on what just happened.

I felt deeply satisfied, wildly embarrassed, mildly dehydrated, and somehow taller all at once.

I couldn’t remember the last time I had used my brain for an end-to-end process without relying on an industrial convenience like a mechanical pencil or Hewlett-Packard toner. I felt total command over your post. I felt crystalline clarity about what I understood, what I didn’t understand, and why a grown man felt moved to alert the entire timeline that he had read a PDF with a pencil. And I was left with unshakable conviction in my POV.

Moreover, I felt the high of “ultra-clean” dopamine.

Not the factory-farmed, seed-oil dopamine you get from pressing a plastic thumb-clicker on a 0.7mm Pentel like a lab rat tapping a lever for pellets. Not the lukewarm, ultra-processed dopamine of reading a contract printed out on bleached 20-pound copy paper that a machine collated for you without even asking you to set the movable type.

No. I’m talking about single-origin, cold-pressed, pasture-raised dopamine. The kind of raw, unadulterated neurochemical high our ancestors felt when they sat down at a mahogany desk, read an actual contract from page one to the signature block, and didn’t immediately open LinkedIn to announce that they had survived the ordeal.

Then I felt embarrassed.

How long had I been depriving myself of turning basic adult errands into sweeping civilizational manifestos?

Just yesterday, I made two slices of sourdough toast without once asking Claude to “review this loaf, break down the crumb structure, and give me feedback as if you’re my baker.” I stood there in front of the toaster like a pioneer on the Oregon Trail, watched the heating coils glow orange, buttered the bread manually, and ate it. And what did I do afterward? Nothing. I just rinsed my plate and went to work. Not a single 1,000-word reflection on the erosion of culinary agency. Not one mention of Socrates. Not one bulleted list of ways to reclaim the sacred space between bread and butter.

I was disgusted with myself.

And then I got curious.

In fact, I got so curious that I had to sit down, because curiosity at this altitude can make a man lightheaded.

Why is it that every time somebody in tech rediscovers an office supply from 1987, he feels spiritually compelled to summon Daniel Kahneman, Socrates, and Viktor Frankl like the Avengers? And what can we do to make sure we don’t surrender our last remaining shred of self-awareness to the Thought Leadership Industrial Complex?

The answer lies in what Daniel Kahneman called System 1 and System 2 thinking, and more importantly, in the three higher systems that Kahneman was too polite to put in the book.

Everyone on the internet loves citing System 1 and System 2, mostly because Thinking, Fast and Slow is the single most-referenced book among people who read a four-page summary of it in 2016 and have been dining out on the phrase “lazy controller” ever since.

System 1 is fast, automatic, and gut-driven thought. It’s what fires when a 42-page commercial agreement lands in your inbox on a Thursday afternoon and your brain immediately says, “I am not reading all of this, I should probably pay an actual lawyer instead of asking a chatbot to roleplay as one.”

System 2 is deliberate, analytical, effortful, and conscious. It’s what fires when you ignore System 1, print the 42-page agreement yourself, grab a mechanical pencil, write “check indemnity??” and “what does mutatis mutandis mean” in the margins for 90 minutes, and walk away from your desk feeling like John Marshall presiding over Marbury v. Madison.

But stopping at System 2 is rookie-level cognition. If you really want to diagnose what is happening to the human mind in 2026, you have to go deeper:

System 3 is performing System 2 in public so strangers know you still have a prefrontal cortex. You didn’t merely read the contract. You observed yourself reading the contract from a cinematic third-person camera angle, felt a single noble tear roll down your cheek, and started mentally workshopping the opening hook somewhere around Section 7.2(b).

System 4 is taking a completely normal Tuesday afternoon task (reading a document before you sign it) and laundering it through one ancient Greek philosopher, three cognitive psychologists, a misattributed quote, ten repetitive bullet points, and a closing comparison to the sun until a routine administrative chore sounds like the drafting of the Magna Carta.

System 5 is reading someone else’s System 4 post and concluding that the only proportionate moral response is to construct an even longer, even more grandiose System 4 post, thereby testing the structural load limits of the X Premium character counter and everybody’s patience simultaneously.

Technology has been hijacking effortful thinking for far longer than 370 BC. Frankly, starting the timeline with Socrates is System 1 history.

Roughly a million years ago: Fire hijacked raw-meat mastication as a gastrointestinal System 2 exercise. Early hominids no longer had to chew elk cartilage for four uninterrupted hours just to extract 300 calories. Immediate metabolic offloading. Everything went downhill from there.

3200 BC: Sumerian cuneiform hijacked remembering how many goats your brother-in-law owed you from the spring harvest. Within two generations, nobody could keep track of a single goat in their head. Pure cognitive atrophy.

1440 AD: Gutenberg’s printing press hijacked the deeply satisfying, hard-fought labor of being a medieval monk squinting in an unheated stone scriptorium for eleven years to hand-copy one manuscript by tallow candle. Did anyone pause to ask what the printing press was doing to the monks’ taste?

1784: Bifocals hijacked squinting as an ocular System 2 exercise.

1822: John Isaac Hawkins and Sampson Mordan secured British Patent No. 4742 for the first mechanical pencil, explicitly designed in the words of the patent itself for “rendering the frequent cutting or mending of the points or nibs unnecessary.”

Stop and sit with that for a moment.

The very mechanical pencil you held aloft yesterday as your Excalibur against Silicon Valley is itself a 204-year-old machine engineered to offload the noble, character-building friction of whittling cedarwood with a blade and blowing graphite dust off your thumb. You didn’t reject shortcuts. You just picked a Victorian shortcut and called it enlightenment.

1959: The Xerox 914 photocopier hijacked retyping contracts on carbon paper.

1983: Microsoft Word hijacked Wite-Out and the healthy, adrenaline-soaked terror of making a typo on page 14 of a 15-page lease.

Calculators hijacked long division.
GPS hijacked arguing with your spouse over a folded Rand McNally road atlas on the center console while missing the exit for Savannah.
Google hijacked sitting at a bar for three hours insisting to your friends that Kevin Costner was in Air Force One when it was actually Harrison Ford, the kind of hard-fought, unadulterated barstool conviction that used to build real character.

Now, to be completely fair to you, you’re right about one big thing. AI really is different.

It doesn’t just take over one effortful job at a time. It takes over all of them at once.

Remembering. Summarizing. Researching. Calculating. Writing. Problem-solving. Weighing trade-offs. Deciding. Planning. Navigating people. Reflecting. Creating. Sounding like a 2019 Medium post. Putting “&” instead of “and” ten times inside a 5,300-character essay where nobody was running out of space. Using the verb “grok” unironically in a manifesto about resisting the machines. Building a ten-item bulleted list where four of the bullets are literally the same bullet wearing different sweaters.

For 200,000 years, our brains have been wired to take the easy out. And when we surrender to shortcuts, whether it’s letting an LLM read our contracts or letting LinkedIn formatting do the heavy lifting of sounding profound, we pay a steep price.

Let’s break down the real costs.

Cost 1: A summary feels like understanding, and a numbered framework feels like wisdom.

You’re completely right that reading a compressed summary tricks your brain into believing you understand a subject you never actually wrestled with. What gets overlooked is the mirror-image trap: taking a twelve-word piece of common sense (“If you don’t read the contract, you won’t know what’s in it”) and inflating it into a 900-word lecture about Paleolithic brain evolution tricks both the author and the reader into thinking they just witnessed a breakthrough in epistemology. Packaging isn’t insight. Single-line paragraphs aren’t depth.

Like this.

And this.

Notice how your brain wants to nod slowly right now, even though I haven’t said anything since the previous paragraph. That’s System 1 getting played by line breaks.

Cost 2: The messy middle is the space for growth, which is also where you discover that reviewing a hefty contract without a lawyer is an exciting way to buy a lawsuit.

Robert Bjork’s work on “desirable difficulties” at UCLA is genuinely great research, and Risko and Gilbert’s work on cognitive offloading is real too. Effortful retrieval makes learning stick. Nobody serious disagrees with that. The funny part is acting like desirable difficulty is an endangered species we have to artificially manufacture with “no-AI blocks,” as if real life isn’t already handing out nine hours of involuntary desirable difficulty every single weekday. Try closing a deal with a stubborn lender, managing a payroll when receivables slip, or reading Section 14.3(c) of a commercial lease where the other side quietly buried a personal guaranty inside a boilerplate maintenance clause. You don’t need a 10-minute productivity hack to experience cognitive friction. Just have actual skin in the game.

Cost 3: The disappearance of judgement, and the rise of the performative sigh.

You asked what will stay uniquely human as we approach AGI and ASI, and you gave us four pillars:

1. Intent
2. Accountability
3. Relationships
4. Judgement

Solid start. Respectable list. A little short, though. If we’re being honest about the final frontier of human uniqueness in the age of superintelligence, there are at least six more traits no neural network will ever truly replicate:

5. Printing a 30-page PDF so you can carry it around the house looking burdened and important.
6. Telling everybody at dinner that you’ve “been going really analog lately.”
7. Buying a $65 brass mechanical pencil from a specialty stationery shop in Kyoto so your margin notes have better mouthfeel.
8. Calling regular job satisfaction “clean dopamine” because saying “I felt good about finishing my work” doesn’t sound like a Huberman episode.
9. Assuming that because you used to outsource your thinking to Claude, the rest of Western civilization forgot how to read a document.
10. Confusing “having taste” with “posting about how important taste is.”

Taste really is thousands of compressed System 2 patterns firing at once. You know what one of those patterns looks like? Reading your own draft back before hitting Post and thinking, “Wait, did I really just compare myself reading a contract with a pencil to fighting for the survival of human thought?”

Cost 4: The Viktor Frankl Industrial Complex.

Every serious productivity essay on the internet must, by federal statute, include the exact quote:

“Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space is our power to choose our response. In our response lies our growth and our freedom.”

It’s a lovely sentiment. There is just one tiny, delicious wrinkle.

Viktor Frankl never wrote it.

Researchers have searched Man’s Search for Meaning and the rest of Frankl’s published works top to bottom. Those words aren’t there. Stephen Covey popularized the line after coming across a similar passage in a university library book in Hawaii (scholars point to psychologist Rollo May’s 1963 writing on pausing between stimulus and response as the closest precursor), and somewhere around the mid-2000s the internet glued Viktor Frankl’s name onto it and never looked back.

Think about the sheer poetry of that. A few lines above your own bullet point commanding humanity to “Read the full source, not the summary,” you dropped the single most famous misattributed summary-culture quote on the entire internet.

If that isn’t a case study in cognitive offloading, nothing is.

Cost 5: The hyperinflation of metaphors.

Once upon a time, a contract was a contract and the sun was a 4.6-billion-year-old ball of fusing hydrogen plasma 93 million miles from Earth that grows crops, powers the water cycle, and gives you a leathery neck if you skip sunscreen on the back nine.

Now a probabilistic text engine that tells you “That’s a really sharp, nuanced point!” every time you misspell a question is “like the sun.”

If AI is the sun, what does that make the mechanical pencil? A patio umbrella? SPF 50? A pair of polarized sunglasses? Once you start comparing software subscriptions to nuclear fusion in space, you leave yourself nowhere to go when something actually important happens.

Cost 6: The collapse of proportionality.

When every minor personal realization (today I read a document carefully instead of skimming an AI bullet list!) has to be framed as an existential battle at the edge of the species, our collective sense of scale breaks down. Sometimes you didn’t strike a blow against the death of thought. Sometimes you just did your homework.

So how do we take back our thinking, our brevity, and our dignity, while still embracing this transformative technology?

It resolves down to one key principle: rebuild the space between having a normal afternoon and writing a 900-word sermon about it.

How you rebuild that space is completely up to you. Pick your poison:

- Create 30-to-60-minute no-AI blocks in your day, followed immediately by 90-minute no-posting blocks so you don’t undo the entire spiritual benefit by bragging about it online.
- Go analog and print out what matters. Then print out something that doesn’t matter at all, just to maintain dominance over your printer.
- Ditch the mechanical pencil. Use a wooden No. 2 and sharpen it with a pocketknife over a metal wastebasket like your grandfather did during the Eisenhower administration.
- Read the full source, not the summary, starting with Man’s Search for Meaning so you can see for yourself which quotes are actually inside it.
- When reviewing a hefty contract, instead of prompting Claude to act “as if you’re my lawyer,” try the radical, ancient analog workflow of hiring an actual lawyer.
- Write your first draft by hand. Write your second draft in wet sand at low tide so you learn non-attachment.
- Set a 10-minute rule: struggle with a problem for 10 minutes before reaching for AI. Then set a 20-minute rule: struggle with the urge to cite Daniel Kahneman before opening X.
- Say it out loud: explain your latest productivity realization to a bartender who cannot legally walk away from his register until you close your tab, and watch his eyes to gauge whether it’s actually profound.
- Memorize a paper highway map and refuse GPS even when you are 18 minutes late to dinner and your wife is staring silently out the passenger window. That icy silence in the front seat? That’s System 2 rebuilding itself in real time.
- Do your own long division on the back of a cocktail napkin at lunch so the table knows you still have skin in the cognitive game.
- Before hitting Post on any essay longer than 500 words, carve it into a slab of limestone with a chisel to test whether humanity truly needed it.
- Replace “grok” with “understand,” replace “&” with “and,” and replace “clean dopamine” with “I felt good about getting my work done.”
- Stare out a window for 15 unbroken minutes with zero inputs, zero podcasts, and zero mental models until you remember that “controlling the space between stimulus and response” used to just be called sitting quietly.
- Never summarize anything again. If a friend asks how a movie was, stand up and recite the entire screenplay from memory with full blocking and lighting cues.
- Treat AI as an “editor,” not a “writer.” That way, when it rewrites every single sentence for you anyway, you can still sleep soundly under the warm blanket of semantics.
- Ask yourself one final question before publishing anything about the future of human cognition: Would Socrates have typed this, or would he have asked for the hemlock twenty minutes early?

AI is like the sun.

Actually, if we’re applying a little System 2 rigor here, AI is nothing like the sun. The sun is a G-type main-sequence star holding eight planets in orbit through gravity that will eventually swell into a red giant and vaporize the earth. AI is a very fast autocomplete machine wired into a warehouse of GPUs that helps people turn a three-sentence email into a keynote about human destiny.

Yes, it may help cure cancer.
Yes, it may put a tutor in every child’s hands.
Yes, it may usher in an age of abundance, starting, apparently, with an unlimited abundance of 900-word essays by executives who just discovered paper and graphite.

It is powerful beyond measure. Which is why we must protect the final frontier of being human at all costs: knowing when to read the contract, put the pencil down, close the laptop, and not write a single word about it on the internet.

Anyway, I’ll be completely honest with you: I didn’t write a single word of this.

I pasted your post into my AI and told it to draft an extremely lengthy quote tweet at least twice as long as yours, because I had better things to do tonight and frankly it seemed funnier than thinking.

We must fight against the death of thought.
